## Why This Is Asked
Crash-resilient PMEM logging is critical for distributed systems and AI/ML workloads on multi-socket servers. This question assesses understanding of durability fences, cache-line ordering semantics, and recovery protocols.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory programming model (PMEM) and its durability guarantees
- Multi-producer single-consumer (MPSC) log semantics and ordering guarantees
- Recovery procedures, CRC validation, and tail-wrapping handling

## Code Example
```c
typedef struct {
    uint64_t seq;    // Monotonically increasing sequence number
    uint64_t len;    // Payload length in bytes
    uint32_t crc;    // CRC-32C checksum
    uint8_t  data[]; // Flexible array member for payload
} pmem_log_entry_t;
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates the ability to design crash-safe concurrent data structures for non-volatile memory, assessing understanding of flush semantics, recovery mechanisms, and performance tradeoffs under contention.

## Key Concepts
- Persistent memory programming model and hardware semantics
- Write-ahead logging and flush primitives (CLWB, SFENCE)
- Per-slot version counters to prevent ABA problems
- Recovery procedures and WAL replay
- Memory ordering and cache-line alignment for performance

## Design Choice: Open Addressing
Linear probing with open addressing is preferred for NVRAM due to superior cache-line alignment, which minimizes unnecessary writes to persistent media, simplified recovery logic without traversing linked structures, and the elimination of pointer overhead inherent in chaining implementations.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of crash-safe memory allocators for persistent memory, including durable data structures, memory ordering, and recovery mechanisms.

## Key Concepts

- Persistent memory semantics and flush/barrier instructions
- Atomic operations (CAS) on a shared free list
- Crash-recovery journaling and idempotent replay
- Per-thread caches to reduce contention
- Memory ordering constraints and cache line alignment

## Code Example

```javascript
// API usage example demonstrates practical implementation
const allocator = new PMEMAllocator(arena);
const block = allocator.alloc();  // Returns 128-byte block
allocator.free(block);           // Returns block to free list
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend this design to support variable block sizes?
- What optimizations would you add for high-concurrency scenarios?
- How would you handle fragmentation over time?

It tests understanding of the Chase-Lev deque, ABA prevention techniques, and the ability to translate algorithmic concepts into correct, high-performance code. Strong candidates will also discuss cache-line padding, false sharing avoidance, and benchmark methodology.
